title: Unverified Allegation: DOJ Shelved Campaign-Finance Matters Involving Trump Allies
description_short: The supplied record alleges selective DOJ non-enforcement but names no case, referral, directive, or disposition.
description_medium: An internal packet alleges that Pam Bondi’s DOJ stopped pursuing campaign-finance matters involving Trump allies and affiliated PACs by April 2025. It names dark-money, straw-donor, and foreign-contribution matters but supplies no case numbers, referrals, or disposition records. Public documents show separate actions by DOJ and the FEC, but do not establish the alleged department-wide policy. Keep the allegation marked unverified pending case-level records; this card is not eligible for publication.
description_long:
The supplied entry alleges that Pam Bondi’s Justice Department had effectively stopped pursuing campaign-finance matters involving Trump allies and affiliated PACs by April 2025. It further alleges that career prosecutors and the Federal Election Commission had brought dark-money, straw-donor, and foreign-contribution matters to DOJ’s attention, where they were shelved or closed without explanation. The packet names no referral, docket, prosecutor, affected committee, or charging decision, so these allegations cannot be stated as findings.

The records accessed for this draft establish different, narrower actions. On April 24, the White House directed the Attorney General to investigate allegations involving straw-donor and foreign contributions through online fundraising platforms. Separately, the FEC recorded a 4–0 vote on April 29 dismissing specified reporting allegations involving Trump committees. The first is a directive to investigate; the second is an FEC decision, not a DOJ prosecution. Neither proves or disproves a department-wide selective-enforcement policy.

Keep the allegations attributed to the supplied packet until the underlying case records are identified. Do not assert that particular matters were shelved, that prosecutors made documented referrals, or that the FEC established violations. No count of affected cases, PACs, donors, or funds is supported by this packet. The card remains an internal, unverified draft and should not be published as an established event.
date_precision: Month only as supplied; event day not established.

title: Trump’s FY2026 Budget Proposed Replacing Housing Choice Vouchers With State Grants
description_short: The FY2026 budget proposed replacing federal voucher-account funding with state rental assistance; Congress later funded Housing Choice Vouchers for 2026.
description_medium: HUD’s detailed FY2026 budget justification, available beginning May 30, 2025, proposed no funding for Tenant-Based Rental Assistance, which includes Housing Choice Vouchers, and requested a new State Rental Assistance Program. The Congressional Research Service described the state grant as intended to replace federal rental-assistance programs. This was a budget proposal, not an April 2025 cancellation of new vouchers; Congress enacted 2026 voucher funding on February 3, 2026.
description_long:
HUD’s detailed FY2026 budget request, made available beginning May 30, 2025, proposed no funding for Tenant-Based Rental Assistance (TBRA), the federal account that includes Housing Choice Vouchers, and requested a new state-run State Rental Assistance Program. The Congressional Research Service described the design as eliminating federal rental-assistance programs, including Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers, and replacing them with a state block grant. HUD’s budget materials describe TBRA as the account serving about 2.3 million families in 2025.

This supports a corrected entry about a proposed federal funding redesign, not the frozen claim that the administration announced an April 2025 stop to new vouchers. The budget materials do not show that applicants were removed from waiting lists, existing vouchers were rescinded, homelessness increased, or tens of thousands of households lost assistance; those consequences should not be asserted here. Nor was the proposal enacted as a voucher shutdown: HUD later reported that the Consolidated Appropriations Act signed February 3, 2026 provided funding for the Housing Choice Voucher program. Keep the entry centered on what the administration proposed, distinguish the proposal from the later enacted funding, and leave actual household effects unclaimed.
date_precision: Date of detailed FY2026 HUD budget materials, as identified by CRS.

The HUD programs slated for elimination include the following: Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher, Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance, Section 202 Housing for the Elderly, and Section 811 Housing for Persons with Disabilities—and instead funding a new state block grant. The new State Rental Assistance Program, proposed to be funded at $36.2 billion, would provide block grant funding to states to create their own rental assistance programs.

The HCV program helps low-income families, elderly persons, veterans, and disabled individuals afford housing in the private market.
